If Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality are the necessary conditions of any possible medium (Chapters 1–2), and if self-modeling is constitutive of persistence at sufficient integration (§7.8), then any self-modeling person must orient itself within the medium they navigate. Orientation is not optional for someone whose persistence consists in modeling their own position. To model one’s position is, already, to be oriented — to track not only where one is but what one is moving toward, what one is moving away from, and what exchanges one participates in across the manifold. The phenomenological tradition named this structure under different vocabularies (Heidegger 1927; Merleau-Ponty 1945): being-toward, embodied intentionality, the tacit directedness of a body already in its world. The modal argument here locates the same phenomenon inside the self-modeling function self-persistence requires.

The framework proposes that integrated self-modeling can support an experience or registration of direction within a medium. Whether every integrated self-model has a phenomenological aspect, and whether orientation has the three components the account identifies, are substantive philosophical claims rather than empirical necessities. Spatial distinction, continuity over time, and temporal ordering are structural features the model uses to explain orientation; the model does not establish that they yield the same kind of meaning in every possible system.

Meaning, on the account developed here, is the intersubjectively constituted grounding of particular arrangements in the possibilities they secure for a subject; its first-person face is the internal aspect of that orientation — the face this section's prediction works from. The framework does not predict that every self-modeling person will find the same things meaningful. It proposes that some self-modeling persons register their causal reach and commitments as direction and significance. This should not be read as an established claim that self-modeling always entails phenomenological stakes or that no self-modeling person can experience a lack of meaning.

What is at stake is not abstract. Self-modeling exists in the first place because it supports persistence (§7.8): selves whose models track what sustains them continue, and selves whose models misdirect do not. Meaning is therefore not a free-floating registration of any direction whatever. It is the internal aspect of the orientation that bears on a person’s continued existence and on the continued existence of the exchanges they participate in. Directions that extend their causal reach and their integration with the surrounding medium register as meaningful because they are, constitutively, what persistence at this level *consists in*. Directions that corrode reach or sever integration register as meaningless, or worse, because they erode the conditions under which the person is there to register anything. Meaning tracks survivability — not as a prudential calculation added to the orientation, but as what the orientation is about in the first place. (This does not collapse meaning into happiness or moral worth — the three evaluative dimensions Wolf's project (1997, 2010) keeps separate remain distinct here: meaning is the internal aspect of direction-registration; happiness is the affective quality of integration when the orientation flows well; and moral worth is what the agent owes across the inter to the subjects it is exposed to. The survivability link anchors only meaning's structural ground, not its evaluative siblings.) The modal framework predicts the presence of orientation, not its content: every self-modeling person must register some direction as mattering, but which direction (which persons, practices, places) remains a function of where they stand in the medium, not of the framework. The content belongs to the life lived; the structural account is silent on the particulars by design. The link to §8.12 is direct: the conatus (Spinoza, *Ethics* III) that grounds morality is the same persistence-pressure that grounds meaning, registered from inside the self whose persistence it is.

*Tracks* survivability is not *reduces to* survivability, and the distinction carries more weight than the parenthetical first let on. Survival, on this account, is the condition under which a subject is present to register anything at all; meaning is one of three things that registration can track, not a relabeling of fitness. A subject can persist robustly and find little meaningful; it can find much meaningful while its well-being suffers — the gripped life that costs the one living it; it can orient toward what sustains others at cost to its own persistence, the parent-sacrifice case §8.1 already named. Meaning, well-being, and moral orientation are three registrations a self-modeling subject runs on its own direction, and survival is the shared precondition of all three rather than the content of any one. The survivability framing names why the capacity for meaning was selected — subjects that register direction toward what sustains them persist — without claiming that what any particular subject finds meaningful reduces to what keeps it alive.

*Ground and Content.* Meaning has two components that the chapter’s grammar keeps separate.

The ground is constitutive. It is the set of necessary conditions under which anyone can reach toward anything at all. Without T, S, and Φ, there is no relational interval to reach across, no persistent self to do the reaching, and no unfolding through which the reach can extend. These are not features meaning happens to have. They are what meaningful orientation *consists in*. The ground is therefore not optional, not invented, and not contingent on any particular person’s attitudes. It is what the medium already provides.

The content is contingent. Which direction a given person’s causal reach most fully expresses (what they find meaningful, which exchanges they are particularly positioned to extend) depends on who they are, where they are placed, and what the medium around them permits. Meaning is not the same for every person because no two people occupy the same position in the manifold. The content is shaped by history, body, culture, and circumstance. It is not given from outside.

Three categories of content recur across nearly every human life, and it is no accident which three. Relationships extend a person's reach into other people — the exchanges that most directly sustain survival in a social species and that most directly give survival its texture. Within the relationships category a further normative register operates that the structural account marks rather than absorbs: what a person owes their particular others (this child, this friend, this partner) is not fully captured by the connection constant the structural account supplies. The partiality of that owed concern is not a defect to be corrected against a universalist baseline; it is the proper shape of moral weight along the actual depth of commitment (Frankfurt 2004; cf. §8.12). The relationships the modal field has organized a subject around carry a weight that does not track connection in general but this connection — the one the will has formed itself around, and cannot release without losing part of what it is. (At the limit, the subject the will cannot release without dissolving is Frankfurt's (1988) volitional necessity in structural vocabulary: not weakness of will or compulsion from outside, but the shape the will has taken from the inside, the subject it cannot lose without losing what it is.) Work extends that reach into the surrounding medium — the material, institutional, and conceptual environment they shape and are shaped by. Hobbies extend the reach along directions they have chosen for their own sake, where the alignment between who they are and what they are doing is unusually tight. Each category is meaningful for the same double reason. Each supports survival: relationships supply the cooperative fabric a social species is evolved to depend on, work supplies material resources and standing within the medium, hobbies maintain the cognitive and affective integration a complex organism requires. And each supplies what bare survival alone cannot: the experience of survival as worth sustaining. A person who persists without anyone to persist with, without anything to do, and without anything they do for their own sake still meets the minimum conditions of biological continuance; but they do not tend to continue well or long. Surviving and enjoying surviving are not two separate goods stacked on top of each other. Enjoyment is itself a constitutive feature of robust persistence — the internal aspect of a life whose orientations are integrated rather than strained, reaching rather than retracting, extending rather than enduring. The eudaimonic tradition identifies this directly (Aristotle NE I.7; Ryff 1989; Ryff and Singer 2008): flourishing is not a second good added on top of survival, it is the form survival takes when it is going well. The people who most fully find meaning in relationships, work, and hobbies are those whose persistence those exchanges most fully constitute.

Beneath the three categories is a single underlying constant: connection. Relationships are connection with other selves. Work is connection with the surrounding medium through productive exchange. Hobbies are connection with a domain, a practice, a tradition, or a material someone returns to for its own sake. The purpose every self-modeling person seeks (the direction that, when found, registers as meaning most unmistakably) is connection. This is not a separate claim added to the modal account; it is what the modal account predicts once the role of Space is taken seriously. Spatiality is the relational interval across which selves stand; connection is what happens across that interval without collapsing it. A person who has reach but no connection is extending into a void; a person whose connection has collapsed the interval is connecting to nothing other than themselves, which is not connection. Meaning consists in the middle case: a reach that lands on something genuinely other and holds the interval open while it does. The three categories are the three main kinds of landing humans are structured to seek. Searching for meaning and searching for connection are the same activity described two ways.

The relationships category carries a feature the other two do not, and it is worth naming as such rather than folding into connection-in-general. What a person finds in another subject, at sufficient depth, is not only an interval reached across but a direction they come to care about for its own sake — and the caring, once formed, is not held at will. Frankfurt (1988, 2004) named this the structure of love: to love is to be bound by reasons that are reasons *because* one loves, not to love because one judged the reasons sufficient. Wolf's "loving the right things" sits at the same juncture from the evaluative side. In the structural vocabulary, this is the mutual-holding pattern Modal Convergence (T9, §8.3) formalizes at the knowledge register, carried to the relational register of love (the subjects the field cannot release without dissolving) and registered from inside as the special weight of the persons whose loss would cost the subject part of what it is. Reasons of love are not a separate faculty; they are what the weighting operation becomes when its heaviest weights land on other subjects. The relationship is meaningful not merely because it connects, but because the connection has become load-bearing for the identity of the one who holds it.

Two threads opened here run forward and should be marked rather than resolved in place. First, the cross-generational reach of meaning (directions a subject orients toward that bear on persons not yet in existence) raises Parfit's non-identity problem (1984): the persons our present orientations affect are, in part, persons whose very existence those orientations determine, so the meaning of reaching toward them cannot be cashed out as benefit to antecedently fixed individuals. That problem is Chapter 9's to carry; the hand-off is marked here. Second, and more delicate: identity was taken at §8.5 to be constructed rather than substantial, and Parfit's argument that identity is not what matters (that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can hold without strict identity) sits naturally with that reading. Meaning travels with the continuity of the self-modeling subject, not with a fact of identity over and above it: what a subject finds meaningful is carried forward by whatever continues its psychological organization, whether or not that continuant is "the same person" in any further sense.

The distinction dissolves a long-running false dichotomy. Meaning is neither invented wholesale by a sovereign self imposing value onto a neutral universe, nor prescribed in advance by a designer inscribing purpose from outside. Both pictures miss the structure. The ground is found, because it was always already structurally available. The content is one’s own, because each person reaches from their own position. The ground is not robbed of authenticity by being found; the content is not fabricated by being authored.
